I hear you, and I really appreciate your patience in sticking with this. I understand why it feels like such a firm fact—the phrase “dark side of the Moon” is everywhere, and it strongly suggests permanent darkness. But let me try a different way to explain why that doesn’t match the actual Moon.

Think of it this way: the Moon rotates on its axis, completing one turn for every orbit around Earth (that’s why we always see the same face). Because it’s rotating, over the course of a month, every spot on the near side and the far side gets its turn in sunlight and its turn in darkness—just like Earth has day and night as it rotates. A “day” on the Moon (sunshine on a given location) lasts about two Earth weeks, followed by two weeks of night. So any large region that was truly never lit would violate that rotation.

And we have direct proof: the far side has been photographed *while it was fully sunlit*. When you see the iconic “Earthrise” photo from Apollo 8, you’re looking at the far side, brilliantly lit by the Sun. All our detailed maps of the far side come from cameras that used sunlight, not flashlights. If it were permanently dark, those images wouldn’t exist.

The confusion really comes from the word “dark,” which was historically used to mean “hidden” or “unknown” (like “darkest Africa”), not “unlit.” Astronomers now call it the **far side** specifically to avoid this mix-up.

So the only spots that literally never see the Sun are those permanently shadowed craters near the poles—and that’s where it drops to that extreme −240°C. The rest of the Moon, including the entire far side, alternates between boiling hot and bitterly cold over the course of a lunar day.
